title: OpenThoughts: Data Recipes for Reasoning Models — Ryan Marten, Bespoke Labs

primary.label: AI Data Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 57%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is SFT distillation for reasoning models, covering teacher selection, data recipe optimization, and fine-tuning methodology. The reasoning models and data recipes apply across math, code, science, and legal domains without a single vertical focus. The talk covers data pipeline construction, SFT model training, and evaluation methodology as integrated stages. Requires familiarity with SFT, RL, chain-of-thought reasoning, and distillation concepts. Recorded conference presentation at AI Engineer World's Fair. Findings are based on ~1,000 experiments with quantitative benchmark results across AIME, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond.

summary: Ryan Marten introduces OpenThoughts, Bespoke Labs' project to build the best open-source reasoning datasets. The motivation stems from DeepSeek R1, whose final released weights are an SFT model (DeepSeek V3 base fine-tuned on 800K SFT examples, 600K reasoning), yet no data recipe was disclosed. OpenThoughts 3 is announced as the state-of-the-art 7B open reasoning model, significantly outperforming DeepSeek R1 Qwen 7B and matching or beating Nvidia's Neimatron nano on math, code, and science benchmarks. The data pipeline involves sourcing questions, mixing sources, filtering questions, generating answers via distillation with a teacher model, filtering bad answers, and selecting the best teacher model. The team conducted roughly 1,000 experiments, creating over 5,000 datasets and nearly 3,000 models. Key learnings include: sampling multiple reasoning traces per question scales 16x with no degradation; Qwen 32B is a stronger teacher than DeepSeek R1 despite weaker benchmarks, possibly due to different reasoning trace length distributions and better formatting; synthetic question sources outperform scraped data and are scalable; question difficulty filtering via LLM labels or response length works better than embedding-based approaches; fewer high-quality sources outperform many diverse sources; and answer verification does not help for general SFT distillation. For domain adaptation, Marten recommends starting with their recipe and iterating, noting optimal choices differ by domain—difficulty labels for code, response length for math and science. He also introduces the open-source Curator library for synthetic data generation and Evalchemy for evaluation. Evaluation is paramount: small evaluation sets should be run multiple times and averaged to reduce noise. A surprising finding is that distillation can surpass the teacher in specialized domains, demonstrated with legal reasoning where a 7B model surpassed R1 on Supreme Court decision classification using 2K questions, 5 samples per question, and answer verification. In Q&A, Marten clarifies the approach is simply regular SFT where answers contain thinking traces, and mentions Claude was a terrible teacher despite being a strong model. Fine-grained reasoning trace analysis was not performed, and interventions to rewrite traces were not helpful.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Case for SFT in Reasoning
sections.summary: Marten introduces the OpenThoughts project and motivates it by noting DeepSeek R1's final weights are an SFT model fine-tuned on 800K examples (600K reasoning), revealing SFT as a practical path to strong reasoning. He notes that reasoning models excel on benchmarks like AIME through long chain-of-thought reasoning. Training one's own reasoning models offers performance, privacy, speed, cost, and ownership advantages.

sections.title: OpenThoughts 3 Announcement and Performance
sections.summary: OpenThoughts 3 is announced as the state-of-the-art 7B open reasoning data recipe, outperforming DeepSeek R1 Qwen 7B distill and matching or beating Nvidia's Neimatron nano on math, code, and science benchmarks. Scaling curves show accuracy increasing with data scale for SFT, and the OpenThoughts recipe shifts the scaling curve upward compared to other open datasets.

sections.title: Data Pipeline and Experimental Approach
sections.summary: The team broke the data pipeline into sourcing questions, mixing sources, filtering questions, generating answers via distillation with a teacher model, filtering bad answers, and selecting the best teacher model. They created over 5,000 datasets and ~3,000 models across ~1,000 experiments, rigorously testing each pipeline decision at small scale before scaling up, mirroring frontier lab methodology.

sections.title: Key Learnings from the Data Recipe
sections.summary: Key findings: multiple traces per question scale 16x without degradation; Qwen 32B outperforms DeepSeek R1 as a teacher despite weaker benchmarks; synthetic question sources outperform scraped data and are scalable; difficulty filtering via LLM labels or response length beats embedding-based methods; fewer high-quality sources beat many diverse sources; answer verification does not help for SFT distillation, possibly because hard problems remain valuable even with incorrect answers.

sections.title: Domain Adaptation and Tooling
sections.summary: Marten advises starting with the OpenThoughts recipe and iterating for domain-specific models. Optimal choices differ by domain: difficulty labels work best for code question filtering, while response length works better for math and science, though response length varies by domain (AIME answers are short numbers, code answers are long). For domains lacking data, synthetic question generation via the open-source Curator library is recommended. Evaluation is paramount for principled data decisions; the open-source Evalchemy library handles evaluation, sharding, and parallelism. Small evaluation sets should be run multiple times and averaged—AIME's 30 questions were run 10 times and averaged to reduce noise.

sections.title: Surpassing the Teacher in Specialized Domains
sections.summary: A surprising and promising finding for domain specialization: distillation can surpass the teacher in some domains, contrary to the assumption that only RL can push the frontier. In a legal reasoning experiment on Supreme Court decision classification, 2K unique questions were sampled 5 times each with answer verification (which did matter here), and the resulting 7B model surpassed R1, a much larger and stronger reasoning model. All resources—paper, weights, datasets, and repos—are openly released.

sections.title: Q&A Session
sections.summary: In Q&A, Marten clarifies that the approach is simply regular SFT where answers contain thinking traces, teaching the model to use its context window for long reasoning. On teacher selection, he speculates Qwen 32B's advantage may stem from different reasoning trace length distributions and better formatting, and notes Claude was a terrible teacher despite being a strong model. On fine-grained reasoning trace analysis, the team did not identify which specific reasoning steps go wrong, and interventions to rewrite traces were not helpful, leaving this as an open research area.
